edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 (page number set apart at the right margin, on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page of the band.

edits.quote: Draw each way on a small shape. (eight recording hexagons printed at half scale, 0.5-inch triangles)
edits.fix: K-1 children have to draw 8 rhombi per covering in 0.5-inch cells, six times. Enlarge the recording hexagons (fewer per page, or a second page), or have children color each rhombus instead of drawing its outline.

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 set. The pieces and boards are all real and printed at actual size, and the band gets actual mathematics: an impossible board with an even number of triangles (the 5-up/3-down trapezoid), fewest greens on triangles (2, 3, 4), fewest blocks where the hexagon is a trap (3 trapezoids beat hexagon plus 3 greens), a placement game whose answers vary (first, second, first, first, second), and finding all 2, 3 and 6 rhombus coverings. All answers check out. The only fixes are the footer and the half-scale recording hexagons in P6, which are too small for kindergarten drawing.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 (page number set apart at the right margin, on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page of the band.

edits.quote: Then explain why nobody can cover the biggest triangle with fewer green triangles than you used.
edits.fix: The biggest (side-5) triangle and the writing lines are on page 4, and nothing on page 3 says so. Write 'the biggest triangle, on the next page' so a child does not stop after the three triangles on page 3.

edits.quote: Imagine a triangle board with 10 small triangles along each side. If you cover it with blue rhombuses and green triangles, what is the fewest number of green triangles you need? What if the board has 100 small triangles along each side?
edits.fix: After the 2, 3, 4, 5 table in P3 this takes seconds of pattern-spotting and cannot hold a child for five minutes. Fold it into P3 as its last question, or make the work explicit: say how to place the blues so that only 10 greens are left, and why fewer is impossible.

edits.quote: Write your numbers in the table.
edits.fix: The table has a 'with blue rhombuses' column that P5 never mentions. Say to copy the Problem 3 numbers into the first column.

edits.quote: Find a rule that tells which places for the two green triangles work, and explain why your rule is right. (three writing lines)
edits.fix: Three lines is not enough for a rule plus an argument in grade 2-3 handwriting. Use the empty space at the bottom of the page for more lines.

grades-2-3.summary: This band develops kernel 1 fully, and every board checks out. P1-P2 give a well-chosen spread: a forced star tiling, odd and even-but-unbalanced impossible boards, two up-holes, a balanced but disconnected hourglass, and a balanced holed hexagon that can be tiled. The rest follows with care: fewest greens (2-5) with a lower-bound proof, chevrons (4, 5, 4, 5, never better than blues), an inverse design problem, and the two-green rule on the side-2 hexagon, which is true for all 144 up/down placements. The edits are small: one problem (P4) is too slight to stand alone, plus a page-break cue, a table instruction and more writing space.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 (page number set apart at the right margin, on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page of the band.

edits.quote: On the small boards below, draw all your coverings from Problem 1 again.
edits.fix: Redrawing the six coverings already drawn in P1 is copying, and drawing lines across a fixed 2x4 grid of boards will be messy. Have children letter their P1 drawings and draw the flip graph with the letters (blank space, or a whiteboard), and drop the eight duplicate boards.

edits.quote: Find a way to do this with 4 flips that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row. (two writing lines, no diagram)
edits.fix: A child has no way to record which hexagons were flipped. Add a small copy of covering A where they can number the hexagons in the order they flip them.

edits.quote: On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges.
edits.fix: The Problem 1 board is also a hexagon, so this is ambiguous. Write 'On the hexagon board from Problem 3'.

edits.quote: Explain why, whenever you make flips and end at the covering you started with, you have made an even number of flips.
edits.fix: This prints the answer to P4's open question ('Can you do it with 5 flips? With 7 flips?'). Ask instead for a proof of the P4 answer: 'Explain your answer to the 5-flip and 7-flip questions in Problem 4.'

edits.quote: Then find the fewest flips that change covering E into covering F in Problem 3, and explain why nobody can do it with fewer.
edits.fix: P3 already asks for the fewest flips from E to F (the answer is 8). Keep only the proof: 'Explain why nobody can change E into F in fewer flips than you found in Problem 3.'

edits.quote: Draw them on the small hexagons below
edits.fix: Drawing all 20 coverings on 0.3-inch grids is about 240 rhombi of copying once ribbons are known. Write 'Draw them or write their pairs of ribbons' so the time goes into the counting argument.

grades-4-5.summary: An excellent treatment of kernel 2, and every drawn covering checks out. Find the 6 coverings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, then its flip graph (diameter 4), then shortest flip routes on the side-2 hexagon (A to B in 3, C to D in 4, E to F in 8), then a 4-flip round trip from A (one exists; 5 and 7 are impossible). The ribbon definition comes with a correct LRRLR example, and the parity and lower-bound proofs lead to two counts of 20 (the 2-2-2 and 1-3-3 hexagons). There is more than enough work. The edits remove copying busywork, a repeated E-to-F question, and a P6 sentence that gives away P4's answer, and add recording space to P4.

overall.strongest: The mathematics is sound and well sequenced in all three bands, from the 2-3 sequence of possible and impossible boards (including the balanced but disconnected hourglass) to the 4-5 path from flips to ribbons to two counts of 20, all on actual-size boards with almost no decorative text.
overall.weakest: Small presentation issues remain: footers missing the id, a 2-3 P4 too slight to stand alone, copying busywork and missing recording space in the 4-5 flip problems, and a 4-5 P6 that gives away P4's answer and repeats P3's E-to-F question.
